activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The library on Delmore Street kept its radiators too high, so Jacob had learned to sit near the periodicals, where a vent poured cold air across the carrels like a slow river. He set his phone face down on the table, which was a kind of subterfuge, since he wasn't studying at all. He was watching the clock inside it. At 4:00 p.m. the admissions portal at Barrington College would update, and either his future would acquire a shape or it would keep refusing him one.

Mandy slid into the chair across from him with a chemistry textbook she had no intention of opening. "You're going to check it here?"

"My mother checks the mailbox every day like it owes her money," Jacob said. "If the letter comes to the house, she opens it before I get home. Here, at least, it's mine."

"So it's not yours at Barrington. It's theirs." She peeled the label off a water bottle in one long strip, the adhesive whispering against the plastic. He noticed she did that when she was nervous, though he never said so, because naming a person's habits can denigrate them, make them seem smaller than they are, and he didn't want Mandy smaller. He wanted her exactly the size she was.

He had found Barrington almost by accident. Back in September, filling out applications at the kitchen table while his mother dried dishes, he'd complained that every school wanted the same essay in a slightly different font. She had leaned over his shoulder and read the top of the website. "The Common Application," she said. "You write once and send it everywhere." He'd clicked the about page to see if that could possibly be legal: it had been founded in 1975 with just 15 member colleges, and now it had more than 1,000. Fifteen schools once, now a thousand. His mother had laughed, a short relieved sound, and said she was glad he didn't have to write twenty separate applications like her cousin had. Jacob had added Barrington that night almost casually, a box checked, a fee paid, the way you buy a lottery ticket to prove you don't care about winning.

He cared about winning. That was the part he hadn't told anyone, not Mandy, not Markus, who had announced over lunch that early decision was binding and Jacob was an idiot for doing it. "It's early action," Jacob had insisted, but he'd gone home and checked, and the word binding sat in the fine print like a splinter. He had applied early decision to Barrington. If they took him, he was going, financial aid or no. He had not corrected Markus. He had not corrected anyone, which was its own kind of lying, and the lie had been sitting in his chest since October, growing quietly the way debt grows.

At 3:58 Mandy said, "Do you want me to look first?" and he almost said yes. He imagined her reading the screen, her face arranging itself into kindness or celebration before she spoke, a buffer between him and the sentence. Instead he shook his head, picked up the phone, and logged in. The page took eleven seconds to load. He counted them by the tick of the radiator, by the smell of old paper and floor wax, by a child two aisles over whispering to a librarian. The screen resolved. There was a confetti graphic, small and looping, and beneath it a line of type.

"Read it out loud," Mandy said.

"'Congratulations on your admission to the Class of,'" and he stopped, because the rest of it was less important than the word admission, which he had not honestly expected, and which now sat in his ears sounding like both a door opening and one closing somewhere else. He put the phone down. His hands were shaking in a way he found embarrassing, and he pressed them flat against the cold table until they were still.

"Jacob." Mandy was frowning at him, at whatever his face was doing. "You got in. Why do you look like you failed something?"

He hadn't shown her the fine print yet. He hadn't shown anyone. He took out a pen, and on the back of a due-date slip he wrote two columns, the way Ms. Walker had taught them in tenth grade for essays that argued with themselves: one side for going, one for staying. In the column for staying he wrote home, and then, after a pause, mom, and then Mandy, no last name needed. The column for going stayed blank longer than it should have, and that frightened him more than the rejection would have, because he could not tell whether the blankness meant he had no reasons or only that he hadn't found them yet.

"Eleven days," he said. "That's how long they give you to accept the binding offer. I found that out tonight." He looked at the two columns, then folded the slip in half and put it in his pocket. Mandy watched him do it and didn't ask which column had won, and he was grateful, because at 4:06 on a Tuesday in a library that smelled of wax and radiator dust, he genuinely did not know.

The child two aisles over laughed at something the librarian said, and the copier behind the reference desk hummed to life.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Orthodox or traditionalist historians of the Cold War, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed its outbreak chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe.
story:
The assignment had been sitting in Felix's bag since Friday, and by Sunday afternoon it had not improved: two historians, one question, who was right about how the Cold War began. He had spread the photocopies across his grandfather's kitchen table, between a bowl of walnuts and a crossword folded to the cryptic page, because his own house was being repainted and smelled like solvent. His grandfather moved around the kitchen making tea and said nothing about the papers, which was one of the advantages of the house.

The first historian argued that the Soviet Union had tightened its grip on Eastern Europe after the war and that the United States had merely reacted. The second argued that American economic ambitions and the atomic bomb had provoked as much as they answered. Felix had read both essays twice, and the trouble was that each one sounded completely convincing while he was reading it. When he put them down, he had nothing. He wanted a judge's verdict, a number, some mechanism that would settle it, and the essays declined to provide one.

"What's all this," his grandfather said, setting down a cup.

"History homework. Two people who disagree."

"Good," his grandfather said. "Agreement is for weather reports." He went back to the counter and left Felix alone with the walnuts.

Felix texted Nancy, who lived four streets over and had the same class. She arrived within half an hour with her own photocopied essay and a bottle of orange soda, and she sat down across from him and immediately began to make the case for the second historian, the one about American ambition, with more confidence than the essay itself contained. "It's obvious," she said. "The Marshall Plan came with strings. They wanted markets."

"Strings for whom," Felix said. "Have you read the part about what happened in Czechoslovakia?" He had only half read it himself, but he had learned in debate club that naming a country you couldn't place on a map was a risky move, so he said it fast.

"You're doing that thing," Nancy said, "where you take whichever side isn't in the room."

"I'm not taking a side. That's the whole problem. I don't know how to take a side."

While they argued, Felix's grandfather came through with a cardboard box he had taken down from the shelf in the back room, the room that smelled of newspaper and glacial drafts from a window that never fully closed. He put the box on the table. "You said homework about the war that wasn't a war," he said. "There's this."

Inside was a thin catalogue from a history museum he and Felix's grandmother had visited decades ago, its cover gone soft at the corners. Felix opened it to the middle and found a photograph of an exhibit panel, the kind with a headline and three short paragraphs, printed in a typeface that belonged to another era. He read the caption aloud, slowly, because the panel's language was strange to him. "It says the traditionalist historians, writing mainly in the late 1940s and 1950s, blamed the outbreak of the Cold War chiefly on Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe."

"That's it?" Nancy said. "One side, all the blame, and they put it on a wall?"

"They call them the traditionalists," Felix said, running his finger under the word. "Also the orthodox."

"So the museum just told everybody the Soviets did it."

Felix sat back. The first of his two historians, the one Nancy disliked, suddenly had a family tree. He hadn't understood, reading the essays side by side, that the argument itself had a history, that the people blaming Moscow had written first and earliest, in the years right after it happened, and that the other argument had come later, answering it. The essays in his bag looked like two men shouting across a canyon, and until now he had assumed the canyon was empty. It was full of other voices, layered, and the catalogue in his hands was one of them, captured under glass in a museum that had also made a choice.

He got his phone and searched, carefully, keeping to the library's site and a university page, and found that the second kind of historian had a name too, the revisionists, and that they had written later, when documents and politics had both changed. He copied the words into his notebook. Nancy leaned over his shoulder, reading, and he could feel her slowing down the way he had slowed down.

"Okay," she said. "So my guy is the comeback. That doesn't make him wrong."

"No," Felix said. "But it doesn't make yours the underdog either. It just means neither one dropped out of the sky." He thought of Mr. Hoang, the retired teacher next door, who had once told Felix over the fence that people who worship certainty usually sublimate their fear of being wrong into a taste for winning arguments. Felix had not known what he meant at the time. He was beginning to.

He pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him and drew a line down the middle. On the left he wrote what the traditionalists had seen, the expansion in Eastern Europe, the timing, the things they had watched happen in front of them. On the right he wrote what the revisionists had brought, the questions about American power, the documents the first generation could not have read. Underneath, where the line ended, he wrote: which explains more of what actually happened, and then crossed out actually and wrote in fact, since the whole trouble was deciding what counted as fact.

The essay he drafted that evening was not the one he had planned. He had wanted a verdict and instead he had written a weighing, evidence set against evidence, with a paragraph at the end admitting that the documents from the Soviet side were still arriving, year by year, and that anyone claiming the matter closed was either lazy or selling something. He thought Nancy would call that relativism, throwing up his hands, and he had an answer ready for her: it was not that truth didn't exist, only that it was not distributed fairly between two rival essays. He would have to be careful not to sublimate his own frustration with the assignment into a fake decisiveness.

His grandfather came through again at dusk, collected the walnut bowl, and paused at the table. He looked at the two columns, the crossed-out word, the line down the middle that ended without ending.

"Verdict?" he said.

"Not yet," Felix said, and turned the page.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: Home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage.
story:
The buzzer at Ines's building stuck halfway, so Vanessa pushed the door with her shoulder the way Ines had taught her, and climbed four flights of stairs that smelled faintly of someone's laundry and someone else's cooking oil. Ines's family had moved into the apartment in September, after months of living with an aunt, and Ines still apologized for the boxes in the hallway even though there was hardly any way around them.

"Careful, that one's my mom's tax stuff," Ines said, leading her past a stack by the kitchen doorway. "She's been crying at the table all week, but if you ask her about it she says she's fine. My aunt says not to pathologize everything, that moving is hard for everybody. But I don't think I'm making it into a disease to notice she's sad."

Vanessa set her bag down. She had come to help Ines study for the chemistry test, speciation and equilibrium constants, but the kitchen table was covered in folders, and at the far end Ines's grandmother sat with a mug going cold, a folder of her own open in front of her. The grandmother lived two floors below in a one-bedroom she had owned for thirty years, and she was, according to Ines, about to sell it.

"Sit, sit," the grandmother said, patting a chair. "Ines, make tea. Vanessa, tell me, are they teaching you anything about money in that school? They taught me nothing. I learned it all by being broke."

Ines filled the kettle, and the grandmother explained it anyway. She had paid off her mortgage years ago, slowly, month by month, on a salary from the hospital laundry. Now a buyer had offered her a price she still couldn't say out loud without pressing her hand flat against the table, as if to hold it down. The whole amount, minus the fees, would be hers. She was moving in with Ines's family for a year to help with rent while she looked for something smaller.

"It's the opposite for Mr. Okafor downstairs," she said. "He sells for the same price and walks away with almost nothing. He still owes the bank most of it. Home equity, Vanessa, is what the home is worth now minus what you still owe on the mortgage. My equity is the whole price. His is barely a sliver."

Vanessa turned that over while the kettle ticked. She had been thinking about her own family's situation all fall, evercest since her mother mentioned, in the flat voice she used for unwelcome facts, that the landlord was raising the rent again. Vanessa had assumed owning and renting were just two different habits, like biking versus walking, and that the difference was mostly about whether you liked moving. But the grandmother's whole sale price and Mr. Okafor's sliver were not two habits. They were two different endings to the same thirty years.

"Wait," Vanessa said slowly, pulling a folder toward her to see the numbers, and the grandmother let her look. "So every rent check my mom pays, at the end there's just the next rent check. But a mortgage payment is partly, like, putting money into the house." She paused, honest with herself about the part she didn't understand. "But at the start, don't you need a pile of money for a down payment? My mom doesn't have a pile of anything."

"Deposit and down payment, two different animals," the grandmother said, ticking them off. "Deposit here is one month, Ines's mother gave it and she fights to get it back when they move. Down payment was my whole savings when I bought, and it took me eight years of saving while renting, which felt like pouring water into sand." She laughed a little, a dry sound. "That is your speciation, for the chemistry girl. Two things that look alike and live apart."

Ines slid mugs onto the table. "Grandma, we have to study. Ms. Mensah will quiz us on the salt calculations tomorrow and Vanessa will sit there looking torpid like she did last week."

"I was not torpid, I was thinking," Vanessa said, but she pulled out her textbook, and the grandmother gathered her folders, folded them into her cloth bag, and stood for a moment at the window, looking down at the street where a moving truck from the old building sat idling with its hazard lights blinking.

"So you understand now, why I can help with the rent," the grandmother said, not quite a question. Vanessa nodded, though the larger thing still wouldn't settle, whether her mother's years of rent counted as nothing or as the ground under somebody's equity. The grandmother patted her shoulder once and started down the stairs with her bag, and Ines opened the textbook to the chapter on solutions, tapping the page. "Equilibrium," she said. "Start with the hard ones."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The party had spilled from Jaya's backyard onto the lawn, and someone's older brother had hooked a phone to the speakers, so that the same four songs kept circling back like birds that refused to migrate. Justin stood near the folding table with his diploma tube under one arm, which everyone kept telling him to put down, and which he kept not putting down. He had worn his gown for exactly one photograph and then folded it into the backseat of his mother's car, and now, in his shirt and the good shoes that pinched, he felt like a stranger at a celebration thrown in his honor.

Jaya found him by the lemonade, which was really just powdered mix and optimism. "You're doing the hovering thing," she said. "You hover when you're thinking too hard, did you know that? You go very still, like a heron."

"I'm not hovering. I'm waiting."

"For what?"

He didn't have an answer, which was itself an answer, so he drank the lemonade instead. The truth, which he had not said to anyone, was that the ceremony had unsettled him. Not the speeches, though those had been long enough that the principal could have expatiated on every graduate by name. What unsettled him was the music. When the first chords rolled out over the gymnasium, half the parents had stood up straighter, and a woman two rows ahead of him had pressed her program to her mouth, and Justin had felt something he could not name move through the whole room at once.

He was still turning it over when Ariane appeared, holding her phone flat like a waiter's tray, its screen showing a grainy recording she'd made from the bleachers. "Listen to this," she said. "I got the whole processional. My grandmother in Dhaka wants to hear it because my cousin graduated there last month and they played the same thing, and she swears it's an American song, and I swear it's English, and neither of us can prove anything because she doesn't text."

Justin put his ear to the phone. Through the crowd noise came the familiar march, stately and unhurried, and then, unexpectedly, a line surfaced in his memory like a coin in shallow water. Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war. He straightened up so fast he knocked the dip spoon into the grass.

"That's Othello," he said.

Ariane looked at him the way you look at someone who has just interrupted a song to identify the composer. "It's Elgar," she said. "My grandmother knows his name. She says English people cry at this."

"It's both." He could feel the pieces fitting, the way they had when Ms. Zhang made them trace a metaphor across three acts. "The title. Pomp and Circumstance. He took the title from Othello. There's a speech, the one Othello gives when he's about to lose everything, where he says farewell to the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war." Saying it aloud, he heard how the phrase carried its own gravity, how it had survived the shipwreck of one man's life and drifted four hundred years into a gymnasium in June.

Jaya had drifted over, and now she frowned at him with her cup halfway to her mouth. "So the song everybody cries to at graduation is quoting a guy talking about war?"

"Not just war. Glorious war. Which is the part that gets me. Othello means it as something he's losing. All the ceremony, the trumpets, the whole parade of his life. It's a farewell. And then somebody sets it to music and we march eighteen-year-olds down an aisle to it like it's a promise." He stopped, aware that he was lecturing at a party, and also aware that he didn't want to stop.

Ariane played the recording again, watching his face this time instead of the screen. "So which is it?" she said. "A farewell or a promise?"

"That's the thing. I think it's both, and I can't make it be one." He looked out at the lawn, at the volleyball someone had abandoned mid-game, at Ms. Zhang, who taught across the hall from his English classroom and was now talking with the parents near the fence. "Yesterday I wanted to be done with this place. Genuinely done, glacial, permanently done. Then the horns came in and I thought, this is the last time all of us are in one room, and the song already knew that. It's not celebrating the war. It's celebrating that you showed up for it."

Jaya set her cup down on the table with unusual care. "Okay, but while you two were having a revelation, I was having a crisis, and nobody noticed." Her voice stayed light, but her shoulders didn't. "Ariane leaves Sunday. Not metaphorically Sunday. Actual Sunday, for the summer program, and then Dublin in the fall, and I have been trying to say something to her since April and I keep swallowing it like a coward."

"What thing?" Ariane said.

"The thing where I say I'm going to miss you and I don't want it to be casual. I didn't want it to be a party thing, over lemonade, but now the party's almost over, so." Jaya exhaled. "That's the thing."

Ariane put her phone in her pocket, which for her was like laying down a sword. She opened her arms, and Jaya walked into them, and the two of them stood on the lawn swaying slightly while the borrowed speaker hissed between songs. Justin turned away to give them the moment, and found Ms. Zhang beside the table, holding out the dip spoon he'd knocked into the grass, washed and dried.

"I heard the Othello bit from over there," she said. "You're the first student in six years who's caught it without being told." She nodded toward the two girls, still holding on. "You might want to do your own version of that before the night's over."

Justin looked at the diploma tube under his arm, and then at Jaya, and then at the darkening sky above the volleyball net. He set the tube down on the folding table at last, next to the lemonade, and walked out onto the lawn.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
The essay prompt sat on the whiteboard in Ms. Wu's classroom like a dare: Explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, and evaluate whether the Federal Reserve's inflation goal makes that job easier or harder. John copied it into his notebook, and beside it, without quite knowing why, he wrote "two percent?" with a question mark that dug through the page.

He had the mechanism more or less in hand by Thursday, or thought he did. Raise rates, and borrowing costs more, so people buy fewer houses and cars, so demand cools, so prices stop climbing so fast. He could recite it in the shower. But when George leaned across the lunch table and said, "Okay, so why do they want inflation at two percent instead of zero? Isn't any inflation bad?" John opened his mouth and nothing came out. The chain of logic in his head ended at a locked door, and behind it was the number itself.

"It's like aiming to be a little bit sick," George said, stealing a fry. "On purpose."

"That can't be the reasoning," John said, though he couldn't say what the reasoning was.

He tried the library after last period. The economics shelves enervated him within minutes; shelf after shelf of glossy textbooks promised "monetary policy made simple" and then buried him in curves. He kept skimming and finding the same sentence, that the Fed "targets inflation," as if the target had fallen from the sky, unnumbered and unexplained. Ines found him there at four o'clock, surrounded by three open books and a growing pile of ones he'd already given up on.

"You look like your phenotype is 'doomed,'" she said, dropping her bio folder on the table. "Recessive, probably."

"Ha." He rubbed his eyes. "I can explain the whole interest rate part. Rates go up, loans get expensive, spending slows, prices calm down. I could teach it. But the essay asks me to evaluate their goal, and I don't even know when the goal became a goal, or what two percent is supposed to be measuring. Was it always two? Did someone vote on it? If I can't say where the number came from, how am I supposed to argue about it?"

Ines, who trusted indexes more than inspiration, flipped to the back of the thickest book and ran her finger down the F's. "Try the entry on the Federal Reserve," she said. "Or there's a chronology in the last chapter."

He found it in the chronology, a single dry line he read three times to be sure. On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. He sat back. Explicit. Before that date there had been no stated number at all, just decades of hints and half commitments, a central bank steering by feel. The two percent hadn't been carved in stone since the beginning; it had been named, on a specific day, by actual people.

"Listen to this," he said, and read the line aloud to Ines, including the whole mouthful at the end. "The personal consumption expenditures price index. That's the yardstick they chose. Not just any inflation number, that one."

"So it's younger than us," Ines said. "Basically."

"That's the part I was missing." He was writing it down now, the date circled twice. "I kept thinking I had to justify two percent against zero, like it was physics. But it's a decision. Somebody sat in a room in 2012 and said, from here on, we say the number out loud." He paused, pencil hovering. "Whether two is the right number, whether hitting it gently with rates actually works every time, I still can't prove that. Maybe nobody can. But at least now I know what I'm arguing about, and what I'm still guessing at."

George found him before first period the next morning. "Did you figure out the sick-on-purpose thing?"

"Some of it," John said, and it was true in a way he found he could live with. "Ask me after I turn in the essay." He slid the draft across the desk, six pages, with the last paragraph beginning: On January 25, 2012, the Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index; what follows is my attempt to evaluate a choice, not a law of nature. Ms. Wu would take it up at the end of class. John uncapped his pen and added one more sentence underneath, small, in the margin.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action.
story:
Mr. Rossi had taped a sign-up sheet to the door of Room 214 on Monday, and by Wednesday every slot was full. Carson's name was third from the top, next to a case name he couldn't pronounce until he'd said it aloud twice in the parking lot: Brandenburg v. Ohio. The assignment was to argue both sides before a panel of seniors pretending to be judges, and Mr. Rossi had made one thing clear at the start. You will not be graded on which side wins, he'd said. You will be graded on whether you can hold both.

"Both," Brody said at lunch, dropping his tray across from Carson. "That's a scam. Nobody holds both. You pick a side and you dress the other one up in a costume."

"I think that's the point."

"The point is Mr. Rossi wants to watch us squirm." Brody stole a fry. "What's the case even about?"

Carson slid the folder across. Inside was a photocopied article about a rally, a speech, an arrest under an Ohio law, and a page of notes he'd taken at midnight, his handwriting getting smaller as it went down. "Some guy gave a speech at a rally. Talked about revenge, march, that kind of thing. They arrested him under a state law that banned advocating violence. The Supreme Court threw the conviction out."

"So the speech side wins. Easy."

"That's what I thought." He pulled the folder back. "But then he has to argue the other side too. And the other side is a state saying, we saw what this kind of talk does, we don't want to wait until it does it again."

Brody chewed on that, and on the fry. "So what's the rule? Where's the line?"

"That's the part I keep losing." Carson tapped his notes. "There's a test. I found it in the opinion, but I can't tell if I'm reading it right."

The library after last period was half empty, the late light coming in flat and gray across the tables. Lila was already there with the case pulled up on her laptop, because Lila did not trust Carson's photocopied articles, and she was right not to. He sat down across from her and she turned the screen toward him without a word.

"Read it out loud," she said. "You'll hear it better."

He read. The Court had held that advocating force could be punished only if it was directed to inciting imminent lawless action and was likely to produce such action. He said the words slowly, once, and then again, and something about hearing them in his own voice seemed to invigorate the whole cramped page. Three conditions, stacked like gates. Directed at inciting. Imminent. Likely to actually work.

"Imminent," Lila said. "That's the load-bearing word. Not someday. Not in general. Right now, this crowd, this minute."

"And likely," Carson said. "The Court isn't just worried about what he said, it's worried about whether the crowd would actually do it."

"So for the state's side, you'd argue the speech met all three. And for the speech side, you'd argue it didn't." She leaned back, nonchalant about it, as if she hadn't just handed him the architecture of the entire assignment. "Where's the trouble?"

"The trouble is the speech is ugly. He talks about revenge, he names an enemy. When I read it I want him punished. Then I read the test and I can't make the words do it." He turned his pencil over and over on the table. "And I have to argue he should be. That's the half I don't believe."

"You don't have to believe it. You have to make it credible."

"That feels like lying."

"It's not lying. It's stress-testing." She closed the laptop halfway. "My mom's a nurse. They argue about etiology all the time, what actually caused the thing, because the treatment depends on it. If you get the cause wrong you treat the wrong disease. You're doing the same thing. What actually makes a crowd break a law, the speech or something that was already in the room?"

The day of the mock court, Room 214 had been rearranged into a rough horseshoe, three seniors at the front with cardboard placards reading CHIEF JUSTICE. Carson stood at the podium with his notes face down, because he'd decided the night before that looking at them would make him lean on them. He argued the state's side first, and it went badly in a way that felt honest. He said the speech was aimed at a crowd already angry, that it was designed to set them moving, that the state could not be expected to wait for windows to break before it acted.

A senior justice with a ponytail cut in. "Designed to set them moving toward what, and when?"

"That's where it gets thin," Carson said, and heard a laugh move through the room, and kept going. "If I'm the state, I say the when is that night, at that rally. If I'm honest, I say I can't prove the crowd was likely to do anything but shout."

"Which are you?"

He looked at the second set of notes, still face down, the side he actually believed, and found that arguing the first side had loosened something in how he held the second. "Both, for right now. The test says advocating force gets punished only if it's directed to inciting imminent lawless action and it's likely to produce it. I think the speech fails the test. I argued that it didn't, and the argument kept sliding out from under me every time I pushed on the word imminent." He turned his notes over. "I could be wrong about likely. That part I can't get to. It depends on what was in that crowd, and none of us were in that crowd."

The chief justice looked at the clock, then at Mr. Rossi, who was leaning against the window with his arms folded and gave nothing away. The chief justice looked back at Carson.

"Time," she said. "Wrap up."

"One sentence," Carson said, and put his notes down on the podium entirely. "The state gets to punish this speech only if it can show all three, and what I learned preparing the state's side is that I couldn't show it, and I'm the one who was trying."

Brody, in the second row, put his hand up for no reason anyone could name and left it there until the chief justice said "That's not how this works," and Brody lowered it, grinning.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
The card in Matthew's hand read AUG, and he had no idea what to do with it. Around him, the community garden was settling into its Saturday rhythms: the old woman by the tomatoes singing to them, Khalil's little sister chasing a pigeon, and Ms. Aziz dragging a folding table out of the shed with the grim patience of someone who had done it a hundred times.

"The final is Tuesday," Khalil said, dealing out cards like a man running a questionable casino. "You failed the last quiz on this."

"I didn't fail it. I got a forty-eight."

"That's failing with style."

Ms. Aziz clapped her hands once. "Right. Khalil has transcribed the DNA sequence onto these cards, which represent messenger RNA, the transcript. Matthew, you're the ribosome today. Duncan's bringing the transfer RNAs."

Duncan came around the bean trellis carrying a shoebox, sweating like a man delivering something illegal. Inside were index cards, each cut in half. The top half had three letters, the bottom half the name of an amino acid. "Ms. Aziz made me write them all out last night," he said. "My hand still hurts. I have a cramp. I'm telling people I got it in a knife fight."

"Tell them you got it in biology," she said.

They taped the messenger RNA cards into a long line along the fence, under the morning glories. Matthew walked it slowly, like a customs officer. AUG. UCG. GGC. AGA. Somewhere, according to the quiz he had failed, each of these triplets was supposed to match up with an amino acid, and the amino acids, joined in order, would make a protein. He understood the outline the way he understood that Montreal existed, having never been.

He picked a card out of Duncan's box at random. UAC, methionine. Held it against AUG. Ms. Aziz, watching from her table, said nothing, which he had learned was her version of applause.

"Wait," he said. "So each of these cards is a tRNA. Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA." He frowned at the card. "So the anticodon is the top half and the codon is what's on the fence."

"There it is," Ms. Aziz said. "Forty-eight percent of the way there."

"She's never going to let that go," Duncan said. "At your wedding she'll stand up and say, the groom once got a forty-eight."

Last summer, before any of this, Matthew had worked the same garden for six weeks, and Ms. Aziz had told him an adage she claimed came from her grandmother: you don't learn a thing by hearing it, you learn it by being slightly embarrassed in public. He had thought this was just her cover for making teenagers weed in July. He had also thought, back then, that he was not a science person, a category he had assigned himself the way people assign themselves a star sign, grandiosely and without evidence. Ms. Aziz had suggested, over the tomatoes, that this was the least interesting thing he believed about himself. He had changed his mind about that somewhere between the zucchini harvest and October, though he could not name the day it happened, which bothered him, because he liked knowing when things happened.

"Okay," he said now. "So I match them. UAC to AUG." He pressed the card to the fence. "And then?"

"Then the amino acid comes off," Khalil said, "and joins the chain, and you move to the next codon. You're the ribosome. Walk."

"I'm a ribosome. I'm a cellular machine, Khalil. I'm basically industrial equipment."

"You're basically a forty-eight."

They built the chain card by card. Matthew walked the fence, matching anticodon to codon, collecting amino acids from Duncan's box, and Duncan kept trying to slip in a card that said PIZZA as an amino acid, and Khalil kept intercepting it, and the pigeon returned to supervise. Twice Matthew mismatched pairs, once with GGC and once with AGA, and Duncan caught it, and the correction was public and slightly embarrassing, exactly as promised.

Near the end of the line, Matthew stopped. "Here's what I still don't get," he said. "The transcript's identical every time. Same DNA, same codons, same order. So how does a cell end up doing different things?"

"That's next unit," Ms. Aziz said.

"So you won't tell me."

"So you'll come Saturday and be slightly embarrassed about it."

Matthew looked at the fence, at the row of paired cards hanging in order like laundry, a protein drying in the sun. He took the last card from Duncan, checked the anticodon against the codon, and clipped it on.

"Fine," he said. "But I'm bringing the pizza card back."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The night before Eid, the kitchen table had disappeared under paper and coins. Alexa's mother had set out the envelope for each family member and was filling them one by one, counting the money twice the way she always did, lips moving but no sound coming out. Alexa sat across from her with her phone face down, which was a kind of discipline, because Elsa had sent eleven messages about the bonfire at the park on Saturday night and every one of them had been more interesting than the envelopes.

"This is zakat al-fitr," her mother said, sliding one envelope toward her. "For you, since you're a member of this family and it's owed for each of us, before the Eid prayer tomorrow." She said it the way she said everything practical, flat as a grocery list, and Alexa took the envelope even though she already knew the name. She had known it since she was eight and had once believed the money itself was somehow holy, that the bills her mother tucked into the flour-sack bag were different from ordinary bills.

Her father came in from the porch with the smell of rain on his jacket, an impermeable thing that had nonetheless let the damp through at the collar. "The Ibrahims first," he said. "Then the family on Delmore, then whoever the imam gave us at the masjid." He was holding a page torn from a notebook, folded twice, the list of people who would receive the envelopes. Alexa understood, and had understood for years without anyone sitting her down to explain it, that the whole point was that these families would get to celebrate Eid too, that the charity was meant to arrive in time for the holiday itself, before the prayer, so that no one would sit out the feast. It was not generosity in the abstract. It had a deadline.

What she had not decided, sitting there with her own envelope warm under her hand, was what she was going to do about Elsa. The bonfire was Saturday night. The Eid prayer was Saturday morning, and after it the whole day would belong to relatives and trays of food and her little cousins shrieking through the house. She could go to the bonfire only if she left early, which meant leaving her grandmother alone at the table with the orange cake she had baked at five in the morning, and Alexa already knew how that scene would go, her grandmother's face folding slowly into something polite and impermeable, no complaint, ever a complaint.

Last year she had skipped the bonfire. She had told Elsa it was family stuff, and Elsa had said that was fine, and then spent the whole night posting photographs in which Alexa did not exist. That small deletion had captivated Alexa in a way she was not proud of; she had studied the photos at two in the morning, counting the faces, noticing exactly where she would have stood. She was still deciding whether the fault had been Elsa's or her own, whether loyalty that is never tested is anything more than a habit.

"I can do the deliveries," she heard herself say. Her father looked up. "The two on Delmore, at least. I want to walk."

"You'll get wet."

"I'll take the good coat."

Her father's eyebrows rose, but he handed her the list, and her mother slid two more envelopes across the table, one for him and one for her, so that Alexa carried four, spread among her pockets like a card trick. Walking the wet streets, she tried to hold both plans in her head at once, the bonfire and the prayer, Elsa and her grandmother, and found they were not actually opposites, only badly timed, which was a different problem and possibly a solvable one, though she could not yet see the solution and was honest enough with herself to admit it.

The family on Delmore was a grandmother and a grown son who opened the door in his socks. He took the envelope with both hands and said Eid Mubarak before Alexa could say it, and behind him a table was already being set, paper plates fanned out like cards, a pot steaming on the stove. The grandmother called something from the kitchen, and the son laughed and translated: she wanted to know if Alexa's mother still made the orange cake. Alexa said yes, tomorrow, and the son said they would have their own sweets tomorrow too, God willing, and it occurred to Alexa, standing in the doorway with rain running off her sleeves, that this was the whole arrangement working exactly as it was supposed to, one family's table making another family's table possible, and that she was the small courier of it.

At home she texted Elsa: prayer is early, I can come after, but I have to be home by eleven. Then, before she could second-guess it, she carried the empty pockets inside, where her mother asked whether the family on Delmore had seemed well, and Alexa said the grandmother asked about your orange cake.

"Tell her she gets the first slice," her mother said, and turned back to her counting.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: NOT EXISTS is another way to find customers with no orders: it keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm monitors and the janitor's lemon cleaner, and Nevaeh had forty minutes before the database unit test she was going to fail. Mr. Mendoza had posted the practice problem that morning: two tables, customers and orders, find the customers who ordered nothing. She had cajoled Marianne out of the last free terminal with a promise of her chemistry notes through finals, and now Marianne was across the room, watching her with the patient look of someone who expected to be repaid in more than notes.

Nevaeh typed her first attempt the way Mr. Mendoza had shown them on Tuesday. LEFT JOIN customers to orders, then filter for the rows where no order matched. The query ran. Zero rows. She stared at the empty result grid, then at the customers table, where she could count at least three names she recognized from the seed data. She ran it again. Zero.

"You're doing that wrong," Miller said from two seats over. He had been quiet until then, headphones around his neck, working on the same problem. She didn't answer, because arguing with Miller was like arguing with the compiler: it never apologized and it was usually right.

"I'm not," she said anyway, quiet, clipped.

"Then why is it empty?"

She looked again. There it was, the thing she'd done without noticing: her WHERE clause sat after the join, and something about the placement was eating her rows before the filter could catch them. She didn't fully understand why yet, and that bothered her more than the empty grid. She dragged the WHERE clause up into the join condition and the result flickered back: two rows. Two customers, no orders.

"Three," Miller said. He turned his screen toward her, unhurried, almost showing off. He had written it a completely different way: NOT EXISTS. "It keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row."

His grid held three names. Hers held two. Same question, same tables, different answers, and one of them was wrong. Nevaeh copied his result into her head and ran the names against what she remembered. He was right. The third customer had no orders either, and her join had somehow lost her, the same silent error she'd made before, just smaller.

"That's mine," she said, before she could stop herself. "You looked at my screen."

"I wrote it before you sat down." He tilted the monitor so she could see the timestamp on his saved file. He had. She felt the accusation fold up in her throat and stay there, and Miller didn't gloat, which was somehow worse. Marianne had drifted over, reading both screens with her arms crossed.

"She's just an apologist for the LEFT JOIN," Miller said. "Defending it even when it's losing rows."

"I'm defending it because it's the one he taught us."

"So use the one that works."

Nevaeh sat with that. Mr. Mendoza had drilled the join method, drawn it on the board, put it on the study guide, and she had assumed that made it the right way rather than one way. Miller's version wasn't a betrayal of the method; it was a second road to the same three names, and both roads were worth knowing on Thursday, because the test didn't care which one she believed in. She still couldn't have said exactly why her first query dropped that third customer. That part stayed open, a door she'd have to walk back through later, and she wrote it on her hand to remind herself.

She opened a second window and retyped Miller's query from memory, letter by letter, until it ran and gave her three rows on her own machine. Then she ran hers beside it, the two grids side by side like a before and after she couldn't fully explain.

"Fine," she said. "Yours works. So does mine, most of the way."

"Most of the way," Miller said, and put his headphones back on.

Marianne leaned in and pointed at the third name on the screen, the customer Nevaeh had missed. "That's the guy who owns the bakery by the bus station. He was in here last week complaining he never gets the promotional emails."

Nevaeh looked at the name for a long moment. "That's because he never ordered anything," she said. "He's in the table, he just doesn't show up."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video had already four hundred shares by the time Carter saw it, and it was only forty seconds long. A warehouse, men in masks, a caption claiming the footage was from last week, from a city two states away, from a raid that had supposedly happened while everyone was asleep. Madyson had sent it to the group chat at midnight with a string of exclamation points, and Israel had replied "this is insane," and Carter had almost pressed share himself before the small hesitation that had been drilled into him all year by Ms. Okonkwo's media unit took hold. He wanted to be the one who checked it. More than that, he wanted to be the one who could tell Madyson, before homeroom, whether she should delete it.

He got to the computer lab early, before Israel arrived, and logged into the machine by the window. The lab smelled like the lemon wipes the janitor used on the keyboards, and the radiator under the desk ticked in a way that made him think of his grandfather's house, though he could not have said why. He pasted the video's link into an image search and waited. The engine returned nothing useful, a page of unrelated thumbnails and a suggestion that he refine his query. He tried again with the link directly, then with the video file downloaded and dragged into the search bar. The engine refused it outright, as though he had offered it a foreign currency.

"You look belligerent," Israel said, dropping his bag on the chair beside him. "What did the computer do to you?"

"It won't search a video." Carter kept his voice low; Ms. Okonkwo was at her desk at the front, marking something with a red pen she held like a conductor's baton. "You can't just paste it in. It wants an image."

"So screenshot it," Israel said, already pulling out his phone.

Carter stared at him. It was so obvious that it felt like a trick. He scrubbed the clip to its clearest moment, the wide shot of the warehouse doors with a truck half visible at the frame's edge, and captured that frame as an image. Then he took two more, one of the masked men, one of a sign on the wall blurred by motion. He dragged the first screenshot into the image search and hit enter.

The results loaded slowly, the lab's connection being what it was, and then the matches appeared like a hand pulling back a curtain. The same warehouse, the same truck, but the sources were news articles dated three years earlier, and the location in the captions was a different country entirely. The second screenshot returned the same set of articles. The third returned nothing, which Carter noted and let go of; two confirmations out of three was enough for the night's claim, though not, he reminded himself, for every claim that would ever cross his phone. He sat back. The video had not been from last week. It had not even been from this decade.

Madyson came in with her headphones around her neck, saw their faces, and stopped. "You found something, didn't you."

"It's old," Carter said. "Like, years old. Different place, too. I took screenshots of the frames and searched those, because you can't run a video through the search itself, and it matched a bunch of articles from before we even started high school."

She looked at her phone, at the share count, which had climbed past five hundred while he worked. "I didn't make it," she said, and there was something defensive in it, something that made Carter think of his cousin, who had once forwarded a fake evacuation notice during a storm and then become, for weeks afterward, an apologist for every chain email he'd ever passed along. Carter had laughed at his cousin then. He did not laugh now, because at midnight, half asleep, he had almost shared the warehouse video too, and the only thing between him and five hundred shares had been a pause he could not take credit for.

"You don't have to delete it," Israel said. "Just post the real story under it."

"I know I don't have to." She pulled out the chair across from them and sat, phone face down on the desk, which was its own kind of decision. "It's just, my aunt already sent it to like six people."

Ms. Okonkwo had drifted over without either of them noticing, her red pen capped and tucked behind her ear. She looked at Carter's screen, at the two sets of images side by side, and raised her eyebrows at him. "Screenshots," she said.

"It was Israel's idea, actually."

"Then Israel gets the good grade and you get the typing." She said it dryly and walked on, and Carter found he could not tell whether she was joking, which was usual, and which he preferred to knowing.

He thought about how much to say in the group chat. He began drafting something long, an itemized takedown, and then deleted it, because he had watched guys at his old school titrate their corrections like that, dropping evidence drop by drop until the other person either caved or exploded, and neither outcome had anything to do with truth. He typed instead: "saw this going around, checked it, it's from a few years ago, different place. happy to show how." He read it twice. There were people in that chat who would call him a fact-checker like it was an insult, and there was a version of him, the one from before this year, who would have enjoyed the fight. He posted the message anyway and watched the screen.

Madyson picked up her phone, scrolled, and after a long moment typed something under her own post. Then she turned the screen toward him so he could see it, the original video with its five hundred shares, and beneath it her comment: "this is old footage, not from last week. taking it down."

"Want to learn the screenshot thing before next period?" Carter asked. "Lab's open till the bell."

Madyson pulled her chair around to his keyboard and said, "Show me the exact frame you used first."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Hannah had the kitchen table to herself, which meant the laptop, the folder of printed notes, and a mug gone cold all counted as her territory until six o'clock. On the screen was the UCAS form, and the form was asking her three questions instead of leaving her a blank page, which was the problem, because every piece of advice she had was built for the blank page.

Her cousin Priya had got into Edinburgh four years ago on the strength of one long essay, shaped like a wave: childhood anecdote, rising interest, wide reading, triumphant conclusion. "Make them remember you," Priya had said on the phone in October. "Start with the fossils." Priya's whole strategy had exhilarated Hannah at the time, the idea that a stranger in an admissions office might be moved by the seven-year-old who cracked open a belemnite on a Dorset beach. She had drafted that opening eleven times.

Then Eunice had come over with her own laptop, sat down across the table, and frowned at Hannah's screen. "Why are you writing it like an essay?" Eunice asked. "For 2026 they changed it. It's not the free-form statement anymore. It's three structured questions. Why you want the subject, and how you've prepared for it." Hannah scrolled up and looked again. The boxes were right there, numbered, patient. She had been so certain of the old shape that she had read the new one as a temporary inconvenience, a formatting quirk, rather than as the actual task.

"I already wrote eight hundred words about the fossils," Hannah said.

"Then cut them up and sort them into the boxes," Eunice said, mouth full of biscuit. "That's what I did. Mine looks boring now but it answers the questions."

"Boring," Hannah repeated, as though the word were a small insult to the fossils. She pushed the laptop a few centimetres away, then pulled it back, and opened the folder of printed notes. Priya's email with the advice was near the front. She read it once more, honestly, looking for what still held. Make them remember you: possibly dead. Answer the question you're asked: alive, and now literal.

The trouble was that the two approaches disagreed about what an admissions tutor wanted. Priya's version trusted atmosphere, a person arriving on the page whole. Eunice's version trusted evidence, a checklist of preparation, reading, an EPQ, the field trip. For an hour Hannah tried to splice them, and the splices were terrible; every paragraph sounded like two people talking at once. She texted Harley, who was applying for engineering and treated all of this with the cheer of someone whose subjects had numbers in them. "just answer the boxes and stop crying," he wrote, followed by, "they changed it because everyone's essays sounded the same anyway."

Hannah put the phone face down and thought about that. If the old essays had sounded the same, then Priya's wave shape was not a fingerprint at all; it was a template dressed up as a personality. Which meant that answering three plain questions might be the more honest version of making them remember you, because the remembering would have to come from what she actually said, not from the architecture around it. She still wasn't sure. The uncertainty sat at the table with her like a third person, and she let it stay, because pretending to be sure had got her eight hundred words in the wrong shape.

She opened the first box and typed: I want to study geology because I have never once been bored by a rock. It was a start, blunt, possibly too blunt. She looked at it, sipped the cold tea, and kept typing: the belemnite, then the reading she'd done after, then the summer course at the university, sorted at last into the question they actually answered. Her nascent plan, that answering plainly could still sound like her, felt less like a strategy than a wager.

At six her mother came in and started heating something in a pan, and Hannah was still writing when the doorbell rang. It was Eunice, back for her charger, which she'd left by the biscuit packet.

"Better?" Eunice asked, leaning over the screen.

"I don't know yet," Hannah said. "Ask me in March." She pulled the charger out of the socket and handed it over, cord still warm.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs: during the US recession of the early 1980s, unemployment rose above 10 percent.
story:
The lemonade stand sat at the end of Adam's driveway, which his mother had pointed out was a bad location, since their street ended in a cul-de-sac and the only traffic was the mail carrier and Mr. Halloran's dog. Adam kept it anyway. He had sixty-one dollars in a shoebox and a summer to fill before college, and filling it with something was better than filling it with nothing.

The problem was Precious. She had biked over at ten that morning, set her helmet on the folding table, and announced that she was going to test him. "You're taking econ in the fall," she said. "I read this thing online about the Fed raising rates, and Felicia says it's all a scam, and I want you to tell me which one of you is right before I decide what to think."

"I haven't taken econ yet," Adam said.

"So take it now. Explain it like I'm a customer."

He poured her a cup and charged her a dollar, because the rules of the stand did not bend for friends. Then he stood there with the pitcher sweating in his hand and realized he had nothing. He knew that the central bank was called the Fed and that it had raised rates last year, and that was the whole of it. "Rates go up," he said, "and, uh, inflation comes down."

"That's not an explanation, that's a weather report."

Felicia arrived before he could improvise, dropped two quarters on the table, and took a cup without asking. "Don't let him burnish it," she said. "It's rich people protecting their money. My uncle says so."

Adam's grandfather had come to stay for the week, and he came out around then with a lawn chair and a thermos of coffee, which offended Adam slightly, since lemonade was right there. He sat down in the shade of the garage and said nothing for a while, which was his way of joining a conversation.

Adam tried again. He had his phone out, skimming, and the pieces were slow to assemble. Higher rates made borrowing expensive, and when borrowing was expensive people spent less, and when people spent less prices stopped climbing. He could feel the shape of it, like a word he almost remembered. "Okay," he said. "Say I want to buy a car. The loan costs more now, so maybe I wait. Everybody waits a little, and the sellers can't raise prices on people who aren't buying."

"So it works," Precious said.

"It works," said the grandfather.

They all turned. He was looking at the cul-de-sac, not at them. "Early eighties," he said. "Rates went way up, and inflation got beaten. People still talk about it like it was a triumph." He took a sip of his coffee. "I was laid off in '82. So was half the plant. Unemployment went above ten percent that year, across the whole country. They teach it as the year we beat inflation."

Nobody said anything. A car turned around at the end of the street, slowed, and kept going.

Adam looked down at his phone, at the chart he had pulled up, and then at his grandfather, who was not looking for sympathy, only stating it, the way he stated the weather. "So it worked," Adam said slowly, "and it cost jobs. Both of those at the same time."

"That's the whole trick of it," his grandfather said. "Nobody mails you a bill."

Felicia put her cup down. "Okay, so I was wrong that it's a scam. But I wasn't wrong that it hurts people."

"They're not opposites," Adam said. "They're the same thing happening." He turned the pitcher in his hands. "The rate hike slows inflation, and the way it slows it is by making the whole economy cold enough that people get laid off. So when somebody praises the hikes, they're praising the part they can see, and my grandpa is the part they can't."

He stopped, because he could hear himself getting florid, the way he did in English class when he was covering for not knowing enough. He was honest enough to admit the gap: he still didn't understand why cooling the economy required unemployment above ten percent rather than above seven, or whether the people who made that decision thought the number through beforehand or simply accepted it. He said so.

"You're allowed to not know things," Precious said. "That's actually more useful than Felicia's uncle."

They sat with that for a while. The mail carrier came up the street and Adam sold him a cup, which made sixty-two dollars and, he thought later, was probably the day's only transaction that was unambiguously good.

His grandfather folded the lawn chair. "Ask me about the plant sometime," he said, heading for the garage. "Not the economics. The plant."

"Okay," Adam called after him. "Tonight?"

His grandfather waved without turning around.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
I am not a nervous person, which is why Kali asked me to help with the truffles in the first place. She gets anxious around boiling sugar, and I do not, and this is a fact about me that I have told her at least ten times, some of them even true. Her kitchen smelled like cocoa the whole way up the stairs, that dark roasted smell that sequesters itself in your coat and follows you home.

"Okay," she said. "The recipe says tempered or it won't snap. It just bends. It goes gray and bends like an old eraser."

"Then we temper it," I said, as if I had done it before, which I had, once, at two in the morning, watching videos instead of studying for chemistry, which I then failed. The videos had shown a woman in Lyon spreading melted chocolate across a marble slab with a scraper, pushing and pooling it, over and over, and I had understood it completely at the time, the way you understand things completely at two in the morning.

Kali's mother kept a marble slab for pastry at the back of the cupboard, and we carried it to the counter by the window, where the light was good and the room was cold because January. The slab was colder than the room, colder than the tile, like a stone you'd find in the shallows of a river. I set a lump of chocolate in a bowl over simmering water and stirred and told Kali about my plan, which was detailed and which I made up as I went.

"It's called tabling," I said. "You spread the melted chocolate on the cold marble and work it around, and it comes down in temperature. That's what starts the right crystals forming." I had not known the word until the video woman said it, but I said it now the way you say a word you've owned for years, and Kali nodded as though this settled something, which it had not, because I still didn't know how cold or how long or how you'd even tell.

The chocolate went glossy and loose, warmer than my wrist. I poured a puddle onto the slab and it sat there, shiny and stubbornly liquid, and I spread it out thin with the scraper, then gathered it back to the center with the flat of the blade, then spread it again. It was like combing a child's hair who keeps turning around. Kali stood at my shoulder narrating, "spread, pool, spread," until I told her that her commentary was hedonistic, and she said that was not what that word meant, and I said fine, it was decadent, and she said that wasn't either, and the chocolate began to thicken under the blade while we argued about vocabulary, which is one way to learn a thing about viscosity.

And it did thicken. Somewhere between my spread and my pool, the sheen dulled to a satin finish and the scraper began to drag, leaving clean tracks that closed slowly behind it, like the wake of a boat crossing a narrow isthmus of chocolate between two pools. I touched the edge of the blade to my lower lip. Barely warm. "Now," I said, with total authority, and swept it back into the bowl with the rest.

Here is what I can tell you honestly, since honesty is apparently my project today: I do not know whether the snap came from the marble or from luck or from the two minutes I spent stirring the seeded bowl in small circles while Kali read the thermometer out loud like a launch announcer. The batch poured into the molds smoothly, without streaks, and when we tested a smear on parchment it set in the time it took to wash the scraper. Maybe I understood the crystallization. Maybe Ms. Goh would have understood it, if she'd been there; she's my chemistry teacher, and once, passing my desk, she said, "Your notes are beautiful and your conclusions are fiction," which I chose to take as a compliment about the notes.

Kali cracked the first finished shard against the counter edge and it broke clean, a small precise sound, like something expensive happening in a film. She held out half without a word, chocolate still cold from the windowsill, and I took it, and we stood there in the cocoa-smelling kitchen listening to the radiators, chewing.

"Tabling," Kali said finally, pointing the other half at the marble slab. "You made that up."

"I did not. Look at the snap."

"I'm looking at it." She ate the rest of hers. "Do the next batch. You explain nothing this time."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
The clipboard in Landon's hand still smelled of the plastic wrap, and the grid he had drawn on it, seven columns for seven days, was half empty because he could not decide what to put in the last two. He stood at the sideline of the outdoor court behind the recreation center while Aleksandar ran layups in the late heat, sneakers scuffing the cracked asphalt, the ball's report echoing off the chain-link fence.

"You're doing the coach thing again," Aleksandar said, catching his own rebound. "You've been standing there for ten minutes."

"I'm making a program," Landon said. "For both of us. Warm-ups, drills, rest days. Everything planned."

Aleksandar dribbled once, twice, and let the ball settle against his hip. "You already work out every day. What's the plan supposed to fix?"

That was the problem, and Landon knew it even if he could not say it cleanly. He had spent the whole summer doing more of everything, and his free throws had barely moved. Ten, fifteen games of one-on-one, shooting until the sky went violet and the streetlights stuttered on. He would come home soaked and satisfied, then lie awake scrolling until two in the morning, his heart palpitating from the third energy drink, and wake up feeling like the court itself, full of cracks. He had a notebook of drills. What he did not have was a single day marked off for nothing.

"Free throws," he said finally. "I've been stuck at around eight for two months."

Aimee arrived with her own ball under her arm and a bottle of gatorade sweating in the heat. She dropped her bag by the fence and read the clipboard upside down. "You've got Monday through Friday full," she said. "Saturday says shooting, and Sunday's blank."

"Sunday is rest," Landon said.

"So what's Tuesday?"

"Warm-up, then ball handling, then conditioning."

Aimee squinted at the grid, then at him. "When do you sleep?"

"Late. You know that. We were on the phone until one-thirty on Wednesday."

She sat down on the bleacher's lowest row and uncapped the drink. "I read something for my sports psych class," she said. "There was a 2011 study at Stanford. Basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed every night. Their free throws went from 7.9 out of 10 to 8.8."

Landon laughed, one short syllable, because it sounded too easy. "Ten hours? Who has ten hours?"

"In bed," Aimee said. "Not asleep the whole time. Just in bed, aiming for it."

Aleksandar shot a free throw and missed it short, the ball clanging off the front rim. He chased it down and came back quieter than usual. "You're saying I'm the problem. Not the drills."

"I'm saying it's part of it," Aimee said.

Landon looked at his clipboard. He had spent weeks building a program that treated his body like a machine with inputs and outputs, and it had not occurred to him that the machine ran on something he was spending until two a.m. He thought about the two approaches the way he'd been taught to hold two arguments in an essay: the planner in him wanted every hour accounted for, and the old summer version of him wanted to play until his hands shook. Maybe the answer wasn't one or the other. Maybe the plan had to include hours that looked like nothing, the same way his Sunday column looked blank but wasn't.

He crossed out Tuesday's conditioning block. In the space he wrote, in small letters, lights out by ten. Then he drew a row across the top of the whole grid and labeled it in bed by 9:30, and under Saturday he wrote warm-up first, then shooting, and after Sunday's word REST he added, no phone.

"You're going to try to be in bed ten hours a night," Aleksandar said. It was not quite a question.

"Starting tonight," Landon said. "We'll shoot fifty free throws each before we leave, and we'll shoot fifty every Saturday for a month, and we'll see."

"You'll turn your phone off at nine-thirty."

"I'll put it in the kitchen," Landon said, "on top of the fridge, next to my dad's obsolescent old alarm clock, the one he keeps saying he'll throw out."

Aleksandar tossed him the ball. "Shoot, then. Baseline. I'm counting."

Landon toed the line, bounced the ball twice, the way he always did, and felt the strangeness of aiming at something that mostly happened in the dark. He released the shot and it dropped through without touching the rim.

"One," Aleksandar said.

Aimee wrote the number on the clipboard with a pen she'd pulled from her bag. "Day one," she said. "Forty-nine to go."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither has a comparative advantage, and Ricardo's model predicts no gain from specializing.
story:
The grocery store on Miller Road kept its dairy case at a temperature that suggested punishment, and Kayla had been standing in front of it for six minutes with her econ textbook propped on a crate of yogurt. She was supposed to be facing the cottage cheese, rotating the older tubs forward, a job Devan had once described as "playing archaeology with dairy." Instead she was stuck on problem fourteen, in which Portugal and England traded cloth and wine, and something about the numbers had begun to itch.

"You're going to freeze in front of the lactose-free section," Devan said, wheeling a dolly of canned tomatoes toward aisle six. "That's how they'll find you. Perfectly preserved. A new phylum."

"Ha," Kayla said, not looking up. "Look at this. Portugal gives up two barrels of wine for every bolt of cloth it makes. Fine. England gives up two barrels of wine for every bolt of cloth too. Same ratio, both sides. But the answer in the back says trade wouldn't help either of them, and I don't get it. England's just better at everything. Isn't that a reason to trade?"

Devan considered this with the seriousness of someone who had once titrated every soda in the break room against cheap instant coffee, just to see. "I got nothing. I drew a boat in the margin of mine."

Russell appeared from behind the cereal endcap, where he had been building a pyramid of oat containers that management would disapprove of and children would knock over by Thursday. "What's the boat for?"

"Nothing. It's a boat." Devan shrugged and pushed the dolly on.

Kayla copied the numbers onto the back of a receipt. Portugal: forty wine, twenty cloth. England: eighty wine, forty cloth. She squinted at them while a woman reached past her for skim milk. England made twice as much of everything, so wasn't England supposed to do everything and Portugal nothing? But that couldn't be right either, because the whole chapter kept insisting that even a country that was terrible at everything could still gain from trade, as long as the costs of making things were different. Different. She underlined it twice, and the receipt tore a little.

"Excuse me, are you an employee or are you studying?" the milk woman asked.

"Both," Kayla said. "Comparatively."

The woman gave her a look reserved for teenagers and left. Russell crouched down next to her, oat pyramid abandoned, and read the receipt upside down, which he claimed was a skill. "Okay so if they both give up the exact same amount of wine to make cloth," he said slowly, "then neither one of them gives up less. Right? That's the whole trick. The one who gives up less of the other thing is the one who's supposed to make it."

Kayla felt the click arrive, the way it did in chemistry when a solution finally turned the color the lab manual promised. "So if Portugal gives up two barrels per cloth and England gives up two barrels per cloth, then nobody's cheaper. Nobody gives up less. There's nothing to specialize around." She flipped to the back of the book again. "Which is why the answer says no gain. It's not that England wins. It's that neither of them has an advantage, because they're identical where it counts."

"Sounds like me and Devan at bowling," Russell said.

"You wish. I'm England, buddy. I'm twice as good at everything."

"No, you're the identical one," Kayla said. "That's the point. You're both equally terrible, so there's no reason for either of you to do the pins and the other one to do the gutter."

Mr. Chaudhry came through on his Thursday shop, pausing at the dairy case with his basket of lentils and one ceremonial bar of dark chocolate. He taught history at the high school and had a way of asking questions that were not actually questions. "Still on the economics, Kayla? Any country yet that refuses to trade out of spite?"

"Not spite. Math," she said, and showed him the receipt, the two matching ratios. "If they give up exactly the same amount, the model says no gain from specializing. Nobody has it."

"Nobody has what, dear?"

"Comparative advantage," Kayla said. "That's the word for it."

He nodded as though she had told him the time, which Kayla had learned was his highest form of praise, and moved on toward the lentils. She stood there a moment longer in the dairy cold, receipt in hand, honest enough with herself to admit that one problem wasn't the whole world. Real countries had exchange rates and politics and Devan's proverbial boats; the model was just a clean room you could think in. Still, it was a nice clean room. She slid the textbook under the cottage cheese crate, where it wouldn't be seen by anyone who mattered, and began rotating the older tubs forward.

Russell returned with a broken oat box, a casualty of the pyramid. "So if we're both equally bad at bowling," he said, holding it up, "do we split the cost of this?"

"No gain from specializing," Kayla said. "You clean it up. You were closer."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Cole had been trying to verbalize the feeling all through the tiebreaker frame, and failing. His heart had gone haywire in the tenth at the bowling alley, when Brennen needed two strikes to force Cole to throw a third, and it was still going now, an hour later, as he held the door of the ice cream shop for Nadia's substitute, a girl named Brennen's cousin, except that wasn't right either, because the girl was Nadia, and Brennen was just the one who had set it up.

"Two scoops or one?" Nadia asked at the counter. She'd beaten him by four pins. She was still carrying the little plastic trophy they'd given out at the lane, a gold thumb with a hole in it, and she set it on the counter like a passport.

"One," Cole said. "Mint." He'd read somewhere, in a unit for Ms. Pereira's class on persuasion, that people trusted speakers who said less. He was testing whether that worked in reverse, whether saying less made him worth trusting. He couldn't decide if that was strategy or cowardice dressed in logos, borrowed logic standing in for an actual personality.

They took a booth by the window. Outside, Donald was skateboarding in the parking lot, waiting, supposedly, for his ride, though Cole suspected he was performing surveillance. Nadia talked first, about the tiebreaker, about how she'd choked the same way at a tournament last spring and had sworn off caring that much about anything with finger holes in it.
