By midnight he had a summary in clumsy Turkish written in his notebook, five sentences, one of which was almost certainly ungrammatical, and a short list of the words he had skipped that he now suspected mattered: terminal, cancelled, until spring.

The next evening he took the stairs down two floors. Mr. Demir's door was already open a little, the way it always was, and the smell of the coffee he always made too strong came out into the hall. Cohen stood there for a second before knocking, notebook in his hand, feeling neither ready nor unready but something between, a kind of blase he did not quite trust himself to be.

"Come in, come in," Mr. Demir said. "You read something for me?"

Cohen sat down on the offered chair, opened the notebook, and started on the ferries. He got through three sentences before Mr. Demir raised a hand, quiet, and asked who had apologized for the delays.

Cohen looked at the word he had never bothered to look up, written in Turkish in his own handwriting, its meaning gone. "I don't know that part yet," he said. "I skimmed."

Mr. Demir poured the coffee and turned the newspaper toward him. "Find it," he said.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
James had dragged the armchair into the corner by the window that morning, angling it so the lamp reached the page without glaring off it, and now the nook smelled of dust and the tea he kept forgetting to drink. Pride and Prejudice lay open on his knee, a photocopy of Chapter Seven beside it, and on the notepad balanced on the armrest he had written two headings in careful block letters: FEMINIST LENS. MARXIST LENS. Under each heading, so far, there was nothing.

The problem was Ms. Tanaka's assignment, due Friday, and the specific instruction that had incapacitated his usual strategy of quoting a critic and paraphrasing: he had to argue something. Not summarize, not admire. Argue, using one or both lenses, in six hundred words. He had read the passage three times, the one where Mrs Bennet explodes at Mr Bennet about Jane and Bingley, and he could not find anything to say that did not feel like saying water was wet.

His phone buzzed against the windowsill. Zaynab: coming over, bringing the worksheet, Jake says he finished already. James wrote "finished already" in the margin and underlined it twice, which was not an argument but felt like one.

She arrived with snow on her shoulders and Jake behind her carrying a grease-stained paper bag as though it were evidence. They folded themselves into the nook, Zaynab cross-legged on the rug, Jake perched on the ottoman, and for a minute nobody mentioned the essay. Then Zaynab said, "Okay, show me what you have," and James turned the notepad around so the two blank headings faced her like an accusation.

"I keep starting from the marriage plot," he said. "Like, Austen's world only lets women move through men, that's the feminist reading, fine. But then the Marxist reading is supposed to be about money and class, and I don't see how I connect them without just writing two mini essays stapled together."

Zaynab pulled the novel toward her and flipped backward, past the passage, hunting. "You're missing the thing underneath. Read the bit where Mr Bennet tells Elizabeth she has an unhappy alternative." She found the page and held it out. "Actually, wait. Jake, you read it last year. What's the entail?"

Jake, who had claimed to be finished, looked at the bag in his hands. "It's like the estate," he said slowly. "Longbourn. It's entailed to a male heir, this guy Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home. Some cousin gets all of it."

James sat forward. "Their own house?"

"Which they're living in," Zaynab said. "When Mr Bennet dies, Collins can throw them out. That's the whole engine of the book, and it's not romance, it's property law."

James took the novel back and found the line, and it was as if the page had been underexposed and someone had finally turned a knob. Mrs Bennet's panic, which he had been reading as a comic flaw, a shrillness to laugh at, was a woman doing arithmetic. Five daughters, no inheritance, one house about to vanish. Her matchmaking, which the narrator kept treating as vulgar, made a cold kind of sense. "So the feminist reading and the Marxist reading aren't two different essays," he said, writing fast now. "It's one system. The money can't reach the women, so the women have to reach the money, and the only route is marriage, and then everyone calls them desperate for taking it."

"That's an argument," Zaynab said.

"Is it mine, though?" He stopped writing. "I mean, I got it from you in ten minutes. Ms. Tanaka's going to know I didn't, I don't know, sweat for it."

Jake reached into the bag and distributed the fried dumplings, which had gone lukewarm in the walk over, and while he chewed he said, "She asked for a lens, not a hallucination. Everything comes from somewhere. Even Austen got her world from somewhere."

"That's either comforting or it's the hedonistic shortcut talking," James said, and Jake grinned, because Jake's entire academic philosophy was that if an idea felt good, he wrote it down and left the doubt for somebody else. James was not sure he could do that. He looked at his two headings and drew an arrow between them, then another arrow down to a new line: the entail is where both readings meet. Then he wrote underneath, in smaller letters, a question he could not yet answer: does Austen criticize the system or only its rudest symptoms?

Because that was the part that snagged. Austen saved her sharpest irony for Mrs Bennet, not for the law that frightened her, and James could not tell whether that made Austen a reformer writing between the lines or a satirist who found desperate women funnier than the men who owned everything. Maybe both. Maybe the book was honest in a way that its author did not entirely intend, like a photograph that catches something in the background.

Zaynab read over his shoulder, her finger hovering above the word entail without touching it. "Leave the question in," she said. "She keeps saying a good essay admits what it can't settle."

Outside the window the snow had thickened, the yard gone featureless and pale, smooth as a steppe under the streetlight. James picked up his pen, crossed out nothing, and added one more line to the page: if Mrs Bennet is right to be afraid, what does it cost to laugh at her?

"I don't know where that goes yet," he said.

"Good," said Zaynab. "Start there and find out."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes.
story:
Gavin carried the last box into his grandmother's house and set it on the radiator cover, where dust coagulated in grey ridges along the edge. The apartment keys sat in his jacket pocket, and the landlord, Mr. Okafor, had texted twice already. "Inspection Thursday. Will deduct as necessary." The apartment had been his for eleven months, and the deposit had been nine hundred dollars, money earned through a summer of hauling mulch, and he wanted all of it back.

He had taken photographs that afternoon before the movers came. Billie had held the phone lamp while he crouched at the baseboards, capturing every scuff, every nail hole where he'd hung the poster of the lake, the small crescent in the kitchen tile where a pan had dropped. "Why are you photographing the bad stuff?" Billie asked. "Isn't that helping him take your money?" Gavin wasn't sure. That was the problem. He only knew that Ms. Henry, the neighbour in 4C, had once stood in the hallway with her laundry basket and said, "Document everything, honey. That deposit isn't his money. It's yours, held in trust until you leave." He hadn't asked what "held in trust" meant. He'd nodded and carried his garbage down.

The next morning at his grandmother's kitchen table, over tea that smelled of bergamot and toast gone slightly black, he spread the photos out and tried to think like two people at once. One of them was his father, who said landlords were thieves with paperwork, that you should fight everything, demand itemization, threaten small claims court. The other was Mr. Okafor himself, quiet and ascetic in his habits, who lived in one room of his own building and patched the stairwell drywall himself rather than pay a contractor. Gavin had watched him do it once, on his knees with a putty knife at eleven at night. A man like that wasn't a thief. But a man like that could still be wrong about what he was allowed to keep.

Declan came by after his shift, smelling of fryer grease, and dropped into the chair opposite. "So what's he saying?" Gavin turned the phone around. The new text read: "Nail holes throughout. Repainting deduction $400. Water stain bathroom ceiling. Remaining deposit $310." Declan whistled low. "Four hundred for paint? Dude. That's the whole game, right there."

"No, look." Gavin pulled up the photos, then a page on his laptop, a tenant rights sheet he'd found at the library because the internet at his grandmother's was a single bar of signal in the front window. "The deposit covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. Small nail holes, that's ordinary. Ordinary aging. He can't deduct for that. In this state, anyway." He said it carefully, testing each clause against what Ms. Henry had told him in the hallway, months ago, her voice going under the hum of the dryer. The stain on the ceiling, though, that was different, and he knew it. The stain was his fault. He'd let the shower curtain hang outside the tub for a semester.

"So you fight him on the paint and eat the stain," Declan said. "Split it in half, basically."

"I don't want to fight him." And that part was true, and it surprised him saying it aloud. His father's voice in his head said tenants who don't fight get eaten. Mr. Okafor's posture, bent over that stairwell drywall, said something else about what a building cost a person. Gavin's own position, he realized, was something neither of them had said: pay for what you actually broke, refuse to pay for the wall getting older. "I'll write it. Not a threat. Just the breakdown."

He drafted it at the window, in the light. The tea had gone cold and a skin had formed across the top of the cup, and he kept writing anyway. He listed the painting charge and stated plainly that small nail holes were normal wear and tear and couldn't be deducted, that he was requesting the itemized statement in writing. For the ceiling, he offered two hundred dollars, or he could come repaint the stain himself with the same primer Mr. Okafor used on the stairwell. He attached the photographs, all of them, timestamped.

Thursday morning he drove back to hand over the keys. Mr. Okafor met him in the hallway, holding a clipboard, a small man with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair. He looked at the printout for a long time. In the silence Gavin could hear Ms. Henry's television through her door, and smell the stairwell's old paint, and somewhere below, a kettle beginning.

"You photograph everything," Mr. Okafor said. It wasn't a question.

"My neighbour told me to."

Mr. Okafor set the clipboard down on the radiator. "The paint I will redo myself anyway. Between tenants. The ceiling, your two hundred is fair." He held out the keys' return envelope, and inside, Gavin could see the check was for seven hundred, not three ten. He signed the walkthrough sheet where the man pointed, his own name looking strange and formal there, like something filed away. Outside, Declan was leaning on the car, and Gavin held up the envelope. "Seven," he said. "Seven," Declan said back.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
The fan above Grandmother's stove had a wobble in it, a small complaint it made every rotation, and Alexia had spread her two articles across the table so that each one sat under a different rhythm of the wobble. The first was from a journal with a glossy cover and a name she could barely pronounce; the second was from something small and plain, the kind of publication Mr. Clarke called "a little shop." Both asked the same question, whether homework improved achievement in secondary schools, and both had landed on her desk because her summer program required her to compare them in a critical review, which was a form of writing she had never attempted and did not yet trust.

Cheyanne arrived first, carrying a bag of cherries and no laptop, which was itself a kind of statement. She pulled a chair around beside Alexia and looked at the articles the way she looked at a menu, quickly, deciding.

"This one's obviously the important one," Cheyanne said, tapping the glossy journal. "Its impact factor is way higher. Higher number, better article. That's just math."

"Is it math," Alexia said, "or is it reputation?"

Annie came in through the screen door before Cheyanne could answer, apologizing for being late because her bike chain had come off twice, and she dropped into the third chair and immediately stole a cherry. Grandmother appeared with a plate of sliced bread and butter and the information that Mr. Clarke would be over later to fix the porch rail, so they should not be alarmed if a strange man started hammering.

Alexia had spent the morning in the sunroom with her grandmother's ancient laptop, and she had found something she wanted to be sure of before she argued. She read the sentence back to herself twice. Then she looked up.

"The impact factor is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years," she said. "That's all it is. It's about the journal, not about any one article in it."

Cheyanne chewed a cherry and considered this with the seriousness of a judge. "So a journal could be famous and still publish one bad paper."

"Or the other way around," Annie said, mouth full. "A tiny journal could have the best paper and nobody cites it because nobody's heard of it."

Alexia felt something shift, not like an answer arriving but like a door swinging open onto a hallway she hadn't known was there. She had been imputing authority to the glossy article all morning, letting the journal's number stand in for the quality of the argument, and the two were not the same thing at all. She said as much, and Cheyanne said "imputing" back at her in a false posh accent until Annie laughed and a cherry pit went somewhere under the stove.

They settled into actual work. Annie took the plain article, Cheyanne took the glossy one, and each of them made a list of claims and evidence while Alexia took notes on the differences. The glossy article was elegant, almost too elegant; its conclusion about homework was sweeping and confident and rested, when they dug, on measures of achievement Alexia couldn't fully trace to their source. The plain article was clumsy in its prose and careful in its bones. It kept admitting things, kept saying "this estimate is uncertain" and "our design cannot rule out," which annoyed Cheyanne, who wanted conclusions, and which Annie defended on the grounds that a person who tells you what they don't know is being honest rather than weak.

"That's like utilitarianism," Annie said unexpectedly. "You know, greatest good for the greatest number. The fancy article wants the biggest effect. The plain one cares about who actually gets helped and whether it's real."

"That is not what utilitarianism means," Cheyanne said.

"It's close enough for a Saturday."

Mr. Clarke knocked at four, carrying a drill and a coffee, and he did not explain anything, which Alexia appreciated more than she could say. He fixed the porch rail, and on his way out he glanced at the table and said only, "Reviews go wrong when the reviewer hides which side they're on. Say your position, then show your work." Then he was gone, and the screen door clapped shut behind him like punctuation.

By evening the three of them had built a paragraph Alexia thought might survive: a position, carefully argued, that the plain article's evidence was stronger even though the glossy article was easier to admire, and that both might be partly wrong because the field moved and certainty was a costume. There was a subterranean worry beneath all of it, a doubt she could feel but not fully name, that her preference for the humble article was itself a bias, a taste for underdogs dressed up as a judgment about method. She put that in the review too, one honest sentence, and Annie read it and said, "You're allowed to not know. It's not a confession, it's a paragraph."

Grandmother turned on the porch light and called that there were burgers. Cheyanne gathered the cherries, Annie retrieved the pit from under the stove with a ruler and considerable pride, and Alexia stacked the two articles together, glossy on top of plain, their differences still unresolved, their argument still halfway hers. She carried them out to the porch, where the new rail held firm, and read her draft once more by the light of the bulb while the first burger sizzled inside.

"Sixteen more words," she said. "Then somebody feed me."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Migration can reshape a pyramid: some Gulf states, such as Qatar, show a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there.
story:
The terminal in Denver was loud in the way airports are, a carpet of announcements and rolling luggage, and Kaitlyn spread her geography project across two plastic chairs near Gate B14 while Emy went to find food. They had left at six that morning, three states in one day, a road trip her mother had framed as college visits and Kaitlyn had understood as a long goodbye. Somewhere outside the windows the Rockies were dissolving into evening haze, but she had her laptop open on her knees and the clock in the corner said 9:47, and the assignment was due at midnight, mountain time or her teacher's time, whichever came first.

The project was Mr. Pelletier's last one, the one he had assigned with that grin of his: pick a country, analyse its population pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Kaitlyn had drawn Chile, with its slow widening at the top like a candle softening, and she had written two clean paragraphs about aging populations and hospital beds. Then Anika had traded her Qatar at the last minute, saying she couldn't spell it, and Kaitlyn had said fine without thinking, because at that point the trade had seemed like a small thing, a favor between friends two weeks before graduation.

Now she stared at the chart and felt a presentiment settle in her stomach, the specific dread of a document that is wrong in a way you can't yet name. The pyramid for Qatar was not a pyramid at all. It bulged enormously in the middle, fat between roughly ages twenty and fifty, and on the male side the bulge was monstrous, a barrel of a graph, while the female side looked almost normal. Below the bulge the bars shrank again, thinning toward childhood. She refreshed the page twice. She checked the source, the UN's own data portal, and then a second source, and then a third, and all of them drew the same impossible shape. Her first thought, embarrassing even privately, was that the whole internet had copied the same error.

Emy came back with a pretzel the size of her head and dropped into the chair across from Kaitlyn. "You look like the chart insulted your family."

"It's broken," Kaitlyn said. She turned the screen. "Look. That can't be real. Where are all the old people? Where are the kids? There are more men in their thirties than everything else combined, basically. It has to be a data error, and I have to submit this by midnight, and I can't analyse a chart that's wrong."

Emy leaned in, chewing, and tilted her head at it the way she tilted her head at modern art. "Huh." She took out her phone and photographed it. "Send it to Anika. She lived over there, didn't she? Her dad did something in Dubai."

Kaitlyn hesitated. Her mother had gone to hunt for a working outlet, and the gate agent was announcing a delay for the flight they were waiting on, the flight bringing Anika's older sister home from her first year away, so Anika was probably circling arrivals in her own anxious orbit. Kaitlyn texted anyway, the photo and one line: is this chart broken or am I losing my mind. Then, because waiting made her introspect in useless circles, she started drafting both versions of the essay in parallel. Version one assumed the error. Version two assumed the error was hers.

At 10:20 Anika called. Kaitlyn put her on speaker between the pretzel and the laptop, and the terminal noise swallowed the first few words until Anika repeated them. "No, it's not broken. That's what it looks like."

"It's what it looks like," Kaitlyn said. "Okay. Why?"

"Some Gulf states have a big bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers live there," Anika said, in the flat, certain tone of someone reciting something she'd grown up around. "Qatar's like that. My dad's compound was all men, engineers and drivers and guys building stadiums. The chart isn't counting people born there. It's counting everyone living there."

Kaitlyn looked at the graph again and the shape reorganized itself in her vision, the way a magic-eye picture resolves, and something somatic happened in her hands, a loosening, her fingers unclenching on the edge of the laptop. The bulge wasn't a population having babies. It was a population assembled, imported, male and working-age, and the thin bars below were the actual citizens' children, and the narrow peak was how few old people there were. "So my whole essay is backwards," she said. "I wrote about nursing homes. Chile needs nursing homes. Qatar needs, what, apartments. Train stations. It needs housing for men in their thirties."

"Sounds like a better essay than the backwards one," Emy said, salt on her chin.

Kaitlyn deleted three paragraphs. The clock said 10:34. She typed fast, and for once the thinking and the typing arrived together, the way they were supposed to. The pyramid couldn't be read as a family tree, she wrote; it had to be read as a census, a snapshot of who was standing on the ground that year, and if you read it that way the question changed. Schools or nursing homes wasn't even the right question for Qatar, though it was exactly right for Chile, and she kept the Chile paragraph as a contrast because the contrast was the point. Two charts. Two entirely different futures. The same assignment.

At 11:52 she proofread with her knee bouncing against the chair leg. Her mother reappeared with a dead phone and a coffee, glanced at the screen, and asked whether she'd learned anything on this trip. Kaitlyn pasted the essay into the submission box and hovered over the button.

"Emy," she said. "If this is wrong, Mr. Pelletier is going to frame it in the hallway as a warning to future seniors."

"Then submit it and go down in history," Emy said, and held the pretzel out like a toast.

Kaitlyn clicked send at 11:58, and overhead the board flickered, and Anika's sister's flight, delayed for hours, finally showed the word she'd been watching for: Arrived.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between large parallel plates the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them.
story:
I am not the kind of person who gets rattled by a clipboard, and I want that on the record before anything else. Mr. Bakker was walking the floor of the museum's electricity hall with his clipboard and his lanyard, checking off names for the placement exercise, and I signed mine with a steady hand. The scholarship paid a disbursement straight into your first tuition bill, two thousand dollars, enough to matter and not enough to gloat about. Emy signed after me and knocked the pen off the table doing it, which tells you everything about the competition.

What I had not told anyone, including myself in any deliberate way, was that the diagnostic we all took on Tuesday had gone badly for me. I said "fine" when my mother asked. I said "fine" to Braden in the parking lot. A person who is fine does not need to say it twice, but that occurred to me only later, at the exhibit, when it was too late to be useful.

The three of us ended up at the same station, two large metal plates standing parallel like the world's flattest bookends, a handheld meter propped between them, and a worksheet clipped to the rail. Mr. Bakker had lambasted Braden in front of the whole class last week for handing in a lab report written as one long paragraph, and Braden was still sore about it, arms crossed, radiating belligerence at the worksheet as if the worksheet had written his grade. "The marked point is closer to the left plate," he said, pointing at the small red dot painted midway up the space between the plates, plainly nearer one side than the other. "So you have to measure to each plate. Obviously."

I took the ruler before Emy could, because the red dot was mine first, and I measured from the dot to the left plate, then from the dot to the right, and wrote both numbers down, and stared at them. They were different. The worksheet wanted one value, the field strength at the dot, and the two distances refused to collapse into it. Emy leaned over my shoulder. I could hear her breathing. I flipped the ruler around, measured again, got a slightly different number, and felt the afternoon start to leak out of me. Somewhere behind us a younger kid was turning a Van de Graaff generator on and off and laughing at his own hair.

"We're allowed to move the probe," Emy said, and that was the thing about her, she always wanted something and it always looked like generosity. Her father worked on the museum's maintenance crew, and she'd told me once that the scholarship kid got their name on a plaque in the lobby, and I had understood perfectly well what that name would mean in a lobby her father mopped. She handed me the meter. I set it at the dot and read the field. Then, because I did not know what else to do with the two distances, I moved the probe to a point midway between the plates, dead center, as far from either plate as you could get, and read it again.

The number did not change.

I moved it back near the left plate. Same number. I said it out loud, slowly, the way you test ice before stepping on it. "Between large plates like these the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges, a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them." Emy wrote it down like it was scripture. Braden said, "Then why did you measure the distances," and I did not answer, because the honest answer was that I had wanted to look busy while my hands were shaking. I erased the distances. The answer needed only the voltage and the gap, and it came out clean, and my hand was steady again, which I noticed the way you notice a bruise you can't remember getting.

Mr. Bakker came around the rail at closing time and read our three worksheets, one after another. He paused on mine longest. "Correct," he said, and then, before I could arrange my face into something modest, he turned the clipboard toward us. "Eligibility requires a passing diagnostic, per the rules. Michael, yours was flagged. It arrived with the wrong cover sheet and hasn't been processed." The floor of the hall tilted slightly, or I did. "Braden, you passed. Barely. Congratulations."

Braden uncrossed his arms. He looked at Emy, then at the red dot between the plates, then at me, and picked up the ruler I had set down. "So do I still need the distances," he said, "or not?"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
Olivier had commandeered the far end of the craft shed by the second day of camp, dragging a table into the corner where the light came through the torn screen and laid a warm stripe across the wood. He was supposed to be making something for the Friday exhibition, like everyone else. Faith was weaving a bracelet that had gone wrong twice. Jameson was assembling a model bridge with more glue than sense. But Olivier had chosen to draw a chair, an actual wooden chair from the mess hall, and by Thursday morning the drawing still didn't look like a chair. The legs wobbled off in directions the real legs never went. The seat floated. He had a whole tablet of failed attempts, and Ms. Somsak, who ran the shed, had already passed his table three times without comment, which he took as its own kind of verdict.

"It's a chair," Jameson said, leaning over his shoulder. "How are you failing at a chair?"

"I'm failing at the chair," Olivier said. "That's different."

Jameson was the kind of person the counsellors called a polymath, half because he actually was good at most things and half because he'd taught himself the word and used it at every opportunity. He could solder, he could argue, he could do the rope course blindfolded. Olivier was good at exactly one thing, which was seeing, and this week it seemed he wasn't even good at that.

He remembered then his grandmother's kitchen, two summers ago, the last summer before she moved to the home. She had sat at her table with a pencil, copying a photograph of the family, and she had said something he hadn't understood at the time: that she drew the counter before she drew the bread on it. He had thought it was a quirk of old age. Now he turned his chair drawing sideways and looked at what he had drawn, and then at what he hadn't.

The spaces between the legs. The gap under the seat where the stretchers crossed. The little wedges of window visible between the spindles of the backrest. They were shapes too. Nobody had told him that in any class he'd ever taken, or maybe someone had and he'd been doodling in the margin. He flipped to a clean page and started again, but this time he drew the empties. The wedge of floor between two legs. The slice of shed wall framed by the seat and the stretcher. He drew the gaps as solid things, dark and definite, and let the chair's outline simply fall out of their edges.

Faith came over and watched him shade a triangle of light between the rungs. "What are you doing?"

"Negative space," Olivier said. "The empty area around and between the subjects of an image. You draw that to get the shape's outline right."

"Draw the nothing," Faith said slowly. "To get the something."

She picked up his earlier attempts, the failures, and laid them next to the new page. The new chair stood. It wasn't better in a way Olivier could name; it was the same chair, the same angles, but it had stopped arguing with itself.

At the evening critique, Ms. Somsak held the drawing up in front of everyone, and Olivier felt the old flare of wanting to be told he was talented. Instead she said, "Tell us what changed." He explained the gaps, the empties, and Jameson, from the back, said, "So you stopped drawing the chair," which was trenchant in the way Jameson often was, cutting precisely to the thing Olivier hadn't worked out yet. Had he? He had drawn the chair, just not first. Or he had drawn where the chair wasn't, and let the isn't-ness define it. Both of those felt partly true, and neither felt complete, and he stood there in front of the group deciding whether to pretend he'd settled it.

"I'm not sure," he said finally. "I drew the spaces and the chair appeared. I don't know which one I was actually drawing."

Ms. Somsak set the picture on the table without correcting him, which he understood was the point.

Later, after lights-out, he sat outside his cabin with the tablet on his knees, drawing by the light of the path lamp. He thought of his grandmother again, her hand moving around the bread instead of across it, and wondered what else she had known and never said, and whether he would have listened. The night air came through the gap between the cabins, cool in the shape of a corridor, and he began, idly, to draw the dark between the two doors.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
Grandfather met them at the door of the house on Kendall Street with his sleeves still rolled up, as though he had been caught in the middle of becoming dressed for the occasion. Inside, the smell of braised pork and star anise had soaked into the curtains and the carpet, and every surface that could hold something red held something red: paper lanterns folded flat against the ceiling fan, couplets pressed to the doorframe with tape that had gone amber, a bowl of mandarins so perfect they looked poured. Jeremy had been to this house maybe a dozen times in his life, always at the edges of things, always the grandson who knew which dishes he liked but not the names of them. Tonight was Lunar New Year, his mother had decided, and they were staying until the end.

After the second course, Grandfather beckoned Jeremy into the kitchen with two fingers and set a stack of empty red envelopes on the counter beside a shoebox of crisp bills. He said something rapid in Cantonese that Jeremy could not follow, and then, slower, "For the little ones. You fill. You give. Good practice." It was less a request than an appointment, and Jeremy acceded to it the way one accedes to being handed something fragile, which is to say he could not imagine putting it down. Grandfather patted the shoebox once, as if introducing it, and went back to his guests.

Anton, seventeen like Jeremy and fluent in a way Jeremy was not, drifted in to help, apparently on the same errand by way of a different parent. They worked side by side, sliding bills into envelopes and writing names in gold ink that dried slowly and smelled like nail polish. There were envelopes for three small cousins Jeremy barely knew. When they reached the one marked Emersyn, Anton peeled off two twenties, aligned them, and had the envelope half open to receive them.

"Wait." Jeremy put his hand out, an involuntary gesture he regretted even as it was still in the air. He was certain and not certain, which was the worst combination, but he had heard it once, clearly, years ago, when his grandmother was folding envelopes at this same counter. "Not forty. Grandma said never four. Four sounds like death, so you don't put it in a red envelope."

Anton looked at the bills, then at Jeremy, and something crossed his face that was not quite ridicule but adjacent to it. "You're sure." It was not a question. Still, he put the twenties back and drew a fifty instead, sliding it in with a small exaggerated care, and Jeremy felt the incipient satisfaction of having been useful curdle almost immediately into doubt, because he could not remember whether the rule he had quoted was something his grandmother had taught him or something he had absorbed and then improved.

Emersyn herself appeared in the doorway holding a plastic cup of chrysanthemum tea, which she was drinking with both hands. She was ten, and she had the solemn manner of a child who has recently decided she is old. "Is that mine?" she asked. Anton sealed the envelope with a thumb and said it was, for later, after dinner. She nodded gravely and withdrew.

The doorbell rang twice before nine. It was Mr. Mendoza from two doors down, holding a net bag of oranges and apologizing for the hour; he had been away and had only got back that afternoon, and he wanted to wish them well for the new year before it got any older. Grandfather took the oranges with both hands and insisted he come in, and for a while the kitchen held four languages being spoken at once, badly, and it was somehow the warmest room Jeremy had been in all year. He filled the last envelope. He wrote the last name. When Grandfather caught his eye across the counter and nodded once, Jeremy understood the nod to mean something like an honorarium paid in trust rather than in money, and he understood also that he might be flattering himself, and he let both understandings sit there together.

The envelopes were distributed after midnight, in the disorder of coats and leftovers. Emersyn opened hers at the table without asking whether that was allowed, counted the fifty with her lips moving, and beamed at Anton. Then she slid off her chair, disappeared into the hallway, and came back with a small red envelope of her own, which she held out to Jeremy with the same gravity she had brought to the tea.

"For you," she said. "Because you helped."

Jeremy took it. It had his name on it in pencil, spelled correctly, and it was thinner than a breath. Behind him he could hear Anton push back from the table to look, and he could feel the whole kitchen slowing down to watch, and when he opened it there were four one-dollar bills inside, folded into a neat square.

He looked up. Emersyn was waiting, radiant, certain she had been generous.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In her 1997 essay on leverage points, Donella Meadows argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, while changing its goals or underlying paradigm changes the most.
story:
The notice went up on Monday, laminated, as though it might otherwise be treated as temporary: the school board proposed a fifty-dollar increase to the annual student parking fee, and the money would fund the expansion of the lot into the strip of woodland behind the gym. Felix read it twice, once for himself and once for the towhee that had been singing from those trees since September, a bird he had no particular feelings about until it became a bird with a price on its habitat.

By Wednesday he had forty signatures on a petition, which sounded impressive until he counted the student body and did the arithmetic. Chanelle, who had organized the petition table, counted it differently. "Forty signatures means forty cars' worth of parents who will call the board," she said, tapping the clipboard. "Parents who vote in the spring. That's leverage." Her leverage, he was beginning to suspect, had a destination: she wanted the fee increased, not defeated, because the surplus after the paving would pay for new theatre lighting, and Chanelle lived in the theatre the way other people lived in their own houses.

The board meeting was held in the cafeteria, under banners from a pasta fundraiser nobody had taken down. Ms. Han, who taught economics and had shown up in her capacity as a taxpayer, took a seat near the back and ate an orange with the composure of someone watching weather. The first hour belonged to the fee itself. A man in a work jacket argued fifty dollars was robbery; a woman argued thirty dollars would be fairer; a third suggested a sliding scale, which struck Felix as kinder and, somehow, beside the point. They were all adjusting a number while the trees waited outside in the dark.

Bianca was seated two rows ahead of him, and during the applause for the sliding scale she turned around. "This is a leverage points problem," she said quietly. "Donella Meadows wrote an essay about it in 1997. She argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much, but changing its goals, or the paradigm underneath, changes the most." Felix looked at her. "Everyone here is fighting over the size of the parking fee," she said. "Nobody's asking what the parking lot is for."

He raised his hand before he had a sentence prepared, which augur well for neither his nerves nor his reputation. When the chair called his name, he stood. He said the fee could be fifty dollars or thirty or free, and the lot would still expand, and the woods would still come down, because expansion was the goal the board had already chosen; the fee was just the sound the goal made when it landed. He said that if they wanted to argue about something, they could argue about whether a school that called itself a green academy should be paving its last copse, or whether the theatre's lighting and the towhee's trees had to be competitors at all. Then he ran out of sentences and sat down.

The chair said his remarks were tangential to the item under discussion, which was the fee. The man in the work jacket, of all people, said the kid wasn't tangential, he was the only one talking about the actual item. Ms. Han said nothing, though she had stopped peeling her orange, and Felix caught her eye long enough to see something that was not approval exactly, more like attention, which in a teacher was rarer.

The board voted to table the fee and revisit the expansion plan, which meant the trees got a stay of execution and Chanelle got nothing, and she let Felix know it in the parking lot afterward with a smile that did most of the talking. "You made my lighting contingent on saving your shrubbery," she said. "That's not strategy. That's martyrdom with a clipboard." He offered her a seat on a new petition, one asking the board to fund the lighting from the district's maintenance reserve, and she looked at him the way one looks at an amateur who has accidentally done something correct.

What Felix could not figure out, walking home past the lot with its pale rectangles of future cars, was whether anything had actually shifted or whether the tabling was just another number being adjusted. Bianca's essay had said the deepest change was the paradigm, and he did not yet know what the school's paradigm was, or whose job it was to notice one. He only knew that the man in the work jacket was still there when he left, standing at the edge of the trees with a flashlight, counting them.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: US employers must generally give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is needed to file a tax return.
story:
I was not at the bank because of the money. I want that on the record before anyone hears it from Jimmy, who tells everything like it's a heist movie. I was there because my mother asked me to deposit her cheque, and because the ice cream shop where I worked all summer had not yet mailed me the form I needed, and those two facts are, strictly speaking, unrelated.

The form is called a W-2. The owner, Mrs. Okafor, had said it over the phone in her nonchalant way, the way she said everything, including "the machine is broken, scoop by hand." She said US employers have to give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is what you need to file your tax return. She said this while a blender roared behind her, so I had to take it on faith, and I had written it on my arm at a red light, which is why my wrist read W-2, END OF JAN, in smeared pen.

That was February the sixth. I am not saying this to complain. I am saying it because dates matter to a person with a plan.

The plan was this: file my return, get my refund, and buy the stand mixer before the price went back up. At the shop I had watched Mrs. Okafor commodify every part of a banana split, the sprinkles measured, the whipped cream from a can because cream by the pint cost too much, and I had decided that if I ever made sundaes for people I loved, I would not do it like an accountant. I had even priced it. The mixer was 249 dollars, plus sales tax, which in our state came to a little over sixteen more, a number I knew because I had kept every receipt from the summer in a shoebox, allegedly for taxes, actually because I liked the way receipts look like tiny formal letters.

Matthieu was already in line when I came in, holding his own paycheque from the garden centre. He showed me the stub. "Look at this," he said. "I worked nineteen hours and they took out money for income tax and for something called CPP, or CPP-like, I didn't read closely. Deductions. Eleven dollars of deductions, Jordyn. What did mine ever do to them."

"They'll give it back, probably," I said. "When you file. If they took too much."

"Who tells you if they took too much?"

The answer, I had recently learned, was nobody. Nobody tells you. You tell the government, using the W-2, which Mrs. Okafor had not sent, which meant the government would never hear from me, which meant, and this was the part that kept me up, the mixer would sell out.

"I'm sure your boss is very organized," Matthieu said, in the tone people use when they have met her.

Behind the counter, Mr. Ferreira, who taught civics at my school and banked here on Thursdays for reasons he called "old habits, like smoking, but with tellers," waved us over while our teller went to find a key. He asked what we were filing. I explained the form, the end of January, wages, taxes withheld, all of it, and he nodded like I had recited a nursery rhyme.

"You're the first student in ten years to know that exists," he said. "Most of them wait until April and then cry in my classroom."

"I don't cry," I said. "I wait by the mailbox. It's different."

Jimmy arrived then, out of breath, holding a receipt for a smoothie and complaining about the sales tax on it, how the menu said 7.40 and he paid 8.25, how the city was nickel-and-diming him into poverty. "You got a whole smoothie," Matthieu said. "I lost eleven dollars and never even saw it." They argued about which was worse, the tax you watch being added or the tax that vanishes before the money touches your hand, and I stood between them feeling like a diplomat at a very small summit.

I would like to say I rose above it. The truth is I had my shoebox of receipts in my backpack, and while they argued I was doing arithmetic on the back of my mother's deposit slip, adding up the summer, the hours, the withheld tax I could see on my own stubs, 62 dollars in total if the stubs were honest, which they were, because machines don't lie, only owners with blenders do.

The teller came back with her key and my mother's receipt, and I stepped up. Behind me Jimmy was still calculating the lifetime cost of smoothie tax. Ahead of me, through the glass, I could see the mailbox on the corner, and in it, statistically speaking, nothing addressed to me yet, though I couldn't be sure. Mrs. Okafor had said the end of January. Mr. Ferreira had not contradicted her. The form was somewhere between her freezer and my future, and the only honest position, the one I had assembled from two arguments and a shoebox, was that the money was mine, that waiting was the tax on waiting, and that if the mixer sold out I would learn to whip cream by hand, which my grandmother had done, and she was an epicure compared to me, honestly, she would have scorned the machine.

"Deposit or withdrawal?" the teller asked.

"Deposit," I said, and slid my mother's cheque under the glass, and behind me Matthieu said, "Wait, go back, who tells you if they took too much?"
